rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father interprets the dream globally: God will select Joseph, and al-Alusi favors the middle view that this means great matters, encompassing the dream's implications.
rows.anchor: كما روي عن الحسن أو للسجود لك كما روي عن مقاتل أو لأمور عظام كما قال الزمخشري فيشمل ما تقدم وكذا يشمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ijtibāʾ is selection; its root suggests gathering something for oneself. One scholar defines divine election as an unearned divine effusion of honors, especially for prophets and the righteous near them.
rows.anchor: أصل الإجتباء من جبيت الشيء إذا حصلته لنفسك وفسروه بالإختيار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative may refer to an election like this dream or to the act of election itself; grammatically kādhalika most naturally qualifies an understood verbal noun.
rows.anchor: ( وكذلك ) في محل نصب صفة لمصدر مقدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proposed parse makes kādhalika the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning 'the matter is so'; al-Alusi says the analysis is unsound.
rows.anchor: وقيل هنا : إن الجار والمجرور خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي الأمر كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father may have withheld the dream's detailed interpretation to avoid spreading it.
rows.anchor: لم يصرح عليه السلام بتفاصيل ما تدل عليه الرؤيا حذرا من إذاعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most treat 'and He will teach you' as a new, emphatic prediction outside the simile; another learned view includes it in the comparison as a further divine honor, which al-Alusi says is possible though less immediate.
rows.anchor: ذهب جميع إلى أنه كلام مبتدأ غير داخل تحت التشبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of taʾwīl al-aḥādīth is interpretation of dreams, which are unseen disclosures God causes sleepers to believe as He wills; the phrase could also encompass true angelic reports or false self-talk and satanic reports.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد من تأويل الأحاديث تعبير الرؤيا إذ هي إخبارات غيبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raghib derives taʾwīl from awl, return: referring something back to its intended meaning, whether in knowledge or action; the source quotes a poetic line using taʾwīl for an outcome.
rows.anchor: وللنوى قبل يوم البين تأويل وجاء الأول بمعنى السياسة التي يراعى مآلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥādīth is an irregular broken plural of ḥadīth, not a collective noun, since its form is one reserved for plurals; al-Zamakhshari calls it a plural in his Mufaṣṣal.
rows.anchor: ( الأحاديث ) جمع تكسير لحديث على غير قياس كما قالوا : باطل وأباطيل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Suddi interpret taʾwīl al-aḥādīth as interpretation of dreams.
rows.anchor: وكون المراد من تأويل الأحاديث تعبير الرؤيا هو المروي عن مجاهد والسدي

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan takes taʾwīl al-aḥādīth to mean the outcomes of affairs.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن أن المراد عواقب الأمور

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj understands the phrase as explaining reports about earlier prophets and peoples and the revealed scriptures.
rows.anchor: وعن الزجاج أن المراد بيان معاني أحاديث الأنبياء والأمم السالفة والكتب المنزلة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view takes the aḥādīth as created spiritual and bodily phenomena and their interpretation as reasoning from them to God's power, wisdom, and majesty; al-Alusi judges these readings non-apparent.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد بالأحاديث الأمور المحدثة من الروحانيات والجسمانيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Completion of favor is variously explained as joining worldly blessing to the next life, adding kingship to prophethood, or adding rescue from ordeals to prophetic teaching; the latter teaching led to Joseph's release and rule.
rows.anchor: وتوسيط ذكر التعليم لكونه من لوازم النبوة والإجتباء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some explain election as high rank, kingship, and esteem among people, and completion of favor as prophethood, the only human office wholly free of deficiency.
rows.anchor: وفسر بعضهم الإجتباء بإعطاء الدرجات العالية كالملك والجلالة في قلوب الخلق وإتمام النعمة بالنبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is possible that the dream itself is God's favor and later blessings complete it, but al-Alusi considers this interpretation remote.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن تعد نفس الرؤيا من نعم الله تعالى عليه فيكون النعم الواصلة إليه بحسبها مصداقا لها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another reading makes election readiness for good, teaching dream interpretation, and completion rescue from hardship; it treats dream interpretation as a sign of prophethood, which al-Alusi disputes because the brothers may have known interpretation and were not prophets.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد من الإجتباء إفاضة ما يستعد به لكل خير ومكرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Proper dream interpretation requires rare knowledge of symbolic correspondences and the ranks of souls; even leading interpreters can err.
rows.anchor: لا يعرف التعبير كما لا ينبغي إلا من عرف المناسبات التي بين الصور ومعانيها

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports a dream brought to the Prophet: Abu Bakr interpreted its canopy, honey, and rope as Islam, Qur'an, and successive rule; the Prophet said he was partly right and partly wrong.
rows.anchor: فقد روى أبو هريرة أن رجلا أتى رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم فقال : إني رأيت ظلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers election to prophethood, teaching the apparent art of interpretation, and completion by rescue from adversity; the father's earlier warning about the dream already hinted at its interpretation and added glad tidings.
rows.anchor: واختير أن المراد بالإجتباء الإصفاء للنبوة وبتعليم التأويل ما هو الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The overall promise is that God will honor Joseph with prophethood and interpretive knowledge, and complete his favor by saving him from hardship; Jacob's family will also be rescued from adversity.
rows.anchor: كما أكرمك بهذه المبشرة الدالة على سجود إخوتك لك ورفعة شأنك عليهم يكرمك بالنبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āl Yaʿqūb means Jacob's family, including his children and others; āl is used for people of standing and differs from the broader ahl.
rows.anchor: وإتمام تعمته عليك ( وعلى آل يعقوب ( بالخلاص من المكاره

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some restrict Jacob's family to his sons and take completion of favor as making them prophets, but al-Alusi says the proposed evidence does not establish their prophethood.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من فسر الآل بالبنين وإتمام النعمة بالإستنباء وجعل حاصل المعنى يمن عليك وعلى سائر أبناء يعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing the brothers as guiding stars indicates that they will guide people, not necessarily become prophets; al-Alusi invokes the report comparing the Prophet's Companions to stars as an example of guidance without that inference.
rows.anchor: ورؤيتهم كواكب يهتدي بأنوارها بمعزل عن أن تكون دليلا على أن مصيرهم إلى النبوة

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A prophetic report says the Companions are like stars and people find guidance by following them; this does not entail that every guide is a prophet.
rows.anchor: فقد قال صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم : أصحابي كالنجوم بأبيهم اقتديتم اهتديتم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One may take the family to be prophets and completion of favor to mean prophethood for them, but the wording also permits different kinds of blessings for Joseph and Jacob's family.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : لا مانع من أن يراد بآل يعقوب سائر نبيه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some prefer taking āl as all Jacob's family because 'your brothers' would be shorter; an objection says 'brothers' could exclude Benjamin, whom the promise should include.
rows.anchor: ورجح بعضهم حمل الآل على ما يعم الأبناء بأنه لو كان المراد الأبناء لكان الأظهر الأخصر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other proposed meanings are Jacob's followers or Jacob himself; al-Alusi regards both as remote, especially the latter.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد بآل يعقوب أتباعه الذين على دينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who take completion of favor as kingship say Jacob's family shares its effects in honor, prestige, and wealth.
rows.anchor: ومن جعل إتمام النعمة إشارة إلى الملك جعل العطف باعتبار أنهم يغتنمون آثاره من العز والجاه والمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibrahim and Isaac are appositional explanations of 'your two forefathers'; God completed Ibrahim's favor through prophethood, friendship, rescue from fire, rescue from sacrifice, or several of these.
rows.anchor: وإتمام النعمة على إبراهيم إما بالنبوة وإما باتخاذه خليلا وإما باتجائه من نار عدوه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: For Isaac, completion may mean prophethood, Jacob's birth from him, or rescue from sacrifice and ransom by a great sacrifice, on the view that Isaac was the intended victim.
rows.anchor: وعلى إسحاق إما بالنبوة أو بإخراج يعقوب من صلبه أو بإنجائه من الذبح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison need not match in every respect; mentioning completion of favor alone can imply earlier favor and thus prior election.
rows.anchor: وأمر التشبيه على سائر الاحتمالات سهل إذ لا يجب أن يكون من كل وجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's knowledge beyond what the dream disclosed may have come from prophetic insight, which often proves true between parent and child, or from revelation.
rows.anchor: ومعرفته عليه السلام ولما أخبر مما لم تدل عليه الرؤيا إما بفراسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is all-knowing and wise, acting according to knowledge and wisdom; this resumptive sentence confirms the preceding promises.
rows.anchor: فاعل لكل شيء حسبما تقتضيه الحكمة فيفعل ما يفعل جريا على سنن علمه وحكمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers here probably mean the same brothers as in the preceding verse, though some allow a broader group because Benjamin also figures in the story; the following 'they said' weighs against that.
rows.anchor: والظاهرة أن المراد بالإخوة هنا ما أريد بالإخوة فيما مر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story contains great signs of God's power and wisdom for those who ask about it or seek lessons; heedless people pass signs without benefit, as in 6:105.
rows.anchor: ( لكل من سأل عن قصتهم وعرفها أو للطالبين للآيات المعتبرين بها فإنهم الواقفون عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account could also prove the Prophet's truth: those who asked him about Joseph received an accurate account without his hearing it or reading a book.
rows.anchor: فالمراد بالقصة نفس المقصوص أو على نبوته عليه الصلاة والسلام الذين سألوه عن قصتهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One view says each section of the story is independently clear proof of Muhammad's prophethood; another says the plural reflects distinct verbal and semantic dimensions of its miraculousness.
rows.anchor: قيل : للإشعار بأن اقتصاص كل طائفة من القصة آية بينة كافية في الدلالة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says 'those who ask' means people generally, with wording that encourages study of a story rich in lessons; al-Alusi considers this and an ellipsis proposal remote.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية : إن المراد من السائلين الناس إلا أنه عدل عنه تحضيضا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Meccan reciters, Ibn Kathir, and Mujahid read 'a sign' in the singular; Ubayy's codex has 'a lesson for those who ask.'
rows.anchor: وقرأ أهل مكة وابن كثير ومجاهد آية على الإفراد وفي مصحف أبي عبرة للسائلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unnamed 'brother' is Benjamin, Joseph's full brother; naming the relationship rather than Benjamin emphasizes that Jacob's love for him was tied to Joseph, and may explain why they did not harm him.
rows.anchor: بنيامين وتخصيصه بالإضافة لاختصاصه بالأخوة من جانبي الأم والأب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax makes Joseph and his brother conjoined subjects, with 'dearer to our father' as predicate; a lām emphasizes the claim, and aḥabb is an anomalous comparative construed with ilā.
rows.anchor: واللام للإبتداء يوسف مبتدأ ( وأخوه ) عطف عليه وقوله سبحانه : ( أحب إلى أبينا منا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says ʿuṣbah is ten or more, from the idea that a group strengthens matters by being bound together; authorities give varying numerical ranges.
rows.anchor: والعصبة والعصابة على ما نقل عن الفراء : العشرة فما زادوا سموا بذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas is reported to define ʿuṣbah as more than ten, or ten to forty; Mujahid says ten to fifteen, Muqatil ten, and Ibn Jubayr six or seven.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أن العصبة ما زاد على العشرة وفي رواية عنه أنها ما بين العشرة والأربعين

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutayba take ʿuṣbah to mean any group, with no singular of the same form; other grammarians give narrower thresholds.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن زيد والزجاج وابن قتيبة هي الجماعة مطلقا ولا واحدا لها من لفظها

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A reading attributed to Ali puts ʿuṣbah in the accusative as a circumstantial phrase with an omitted predicate; Ibn al-Munir's alternative ellipsis is rejected because the wording gives no clear clue.
rows.anchor: وروي النزال بن سبرة عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه أنه قرأ بنصب ( عصبة )

rows.speaker: الفرزدق
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers the analogy of al-Farazdaq's 'your judgment is established,' where an omitted clause is understood from context; he says Ali's reading is even more irregular.
rows.anchor: والأولى أن يعتبر نظير قول الفرزدق : + يا لهذم حكمك مسمطا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Our father is clearly in error' means, in their mistaken view, that Jacob misjudges how to apportion affection and fails to give each child his proper place; 'manifest' stresses how obvious they think it is.
rows.anchor: أي خطأ في الرأي وذهاب عن طريق التعديل اللائق من تنزيل كل منا منزلته

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi's account says Jacob loved Joseph because he saw signs of promise in him; the dream further increased that love and the brothers' envy.
rows.anchor: وكانت إخوته يحسدونه فلما رأى الرؤيا تضاعفت له المحبة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some attribute Jacob's greater affection to Joseph's youth and his mother's death, supported by a poem about the youngest child; al-Alusi objects that Benjamin was younger and the verse points to Joseph's full-brother bond.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : إن سبب زيادة حبه عليه السلام ليوسف وأخيه صغرهما وموت أمهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob favored Joseph because he saw good qualities absent from the others, and the dream confirmed those signs; unequal affection itself is not blameworthy when beyond human control.
rows.anchor: فالذي ينبغي أن يعول عليه أنه عليه السلام إنما أحبه أكثر منهم لما رأى فيه من مخايل الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers apparently treated Jacob's preference as a fallible judgment, resolving how they could criticize him without denying his prophethood or becoming unbelievers.
rows.anchor: نعم ظن أبناؤه أن ما كان منه عليه السلام إنما كان عن اجتهاد وأنه قد أخطأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposal to kill or exile Joseph was likely made by one brother to the others, who agreed except the later dissenter; it may have been voiced by all. An outside adviser is possible but unsupported and contrary to the apparent reading.
rows.anchor: ( اقتلوا يوسف أو اطرحوه أرضا الظاهر أن هذا من جملة ما حكى بعد قوله سبحانه : ( إذ قالوا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They offer either murder or throwing him into a distant land; 'earth' may be an object after an omitted preposition, a second object of a verb implying removal, or a locative, though the last is disputed.
rows.anchor: ونصب ( أرضا ) على إسقاط حرف الجر كما ذهب إليه الحوفي وابن عطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exile would achieve separation like killing while avoiding murder's sin; 'may your father's face be free for you' is a suggestive metonymy for his undivided affection, which al-Alusi finds best.
rows.anchor: والمراد سلامة محبته لهم ممن يشاركهم فيها وينازعهم إياها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'After him' can mean after they finish with Joseph, after killing or casting him away; the pronoun may refer to Joseph or to the implied act.
rows.anchor: فالضمير إما ليوسف أو لأحد المصدرين المفهومين من الفعلين

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi and the majority explain becoming righteous as repenting to God for their sin.
rows.anchor: بالتوبة والتنصل إلى الله تعالى عما جئتم به من الذنب كما روي عن الكلبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Righteousness could mean making peace with their father by an excuse, though the lie would remain sinful; alternatively, it means worldly affairs will prosper once their father's attention is theirs.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن المراد ذلك لكن بينهم وبين أبيهم بالعذر وهو وإن كان مخالفا للدين لكونه كذبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing the brothers' own benefit as 'for you' and repeating it is persuasive because people are most attentive to their own interests.
rows.anchor: وإيثار الخطاب في ( لكم ) وما بعده للمبالغة في حملهم على القبول

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi identifies the dissenter as Judah, whose proposal was the least harmful; Ibn Ishaq says Reuben, Mujahid says Simeon, and others say Dan. Al-Alusi considers Judah most likely.
rows.anchor: وهو يهوذا وكان رأيه فيه أهون شرا من رأي غيره وهو القائل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid names Simeon as the brother who spoke against killing Joseph.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد أنه شمعون وقيل : دان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the Qur'an omits names to shield wrongdoers, since all brothers sinned to varying degrees; al-Alusi rejects the claim that commentators therefore must not identify them.
rows.anchor: قيل : وإنما لم يذكر أحد منهم باسمه سترا على المسيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence answers an implied question about whether anyone dissented; saying 'Joseph' rather than 'him' stirs compassion and highlights the gravity of killing him.
rows.anchor: والإتيان بيوسف دون ضميره لاستجلاب شفقتهم عليه واستعظام قتله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayābat al-jubb is the well's hidden depth; al-Harawi instead describes a recess or alcove above the water, while jubb is an unlined well and a lined one is a biʾr.
rows.anchor: وقال الهروي : الغيابة في الجب شبه كهف أو طاق في البئر فوق الماء

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nafiʿ reads ghiyābāt in both occurrences, suggesting several recesses or a generic well; Ibn Hurmuz doubles the yāʾ, Hasan reads ghayābah, and Ubayy's codex has ghaybah.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع في غيابات في الموضعين كأن لتلك الجب غيابات ففيه إشارة إلى سعتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iltiqāṭ is taking up something exposed to loss, with the aim of preserving it; al-Majmaʿ says it is finding and taking an object without searching for it.
rows.anchor: أي يأخذه على وجه الصيانة عن الضياع والتلف فإن الالتقاط أخذ شيء مشرف على الضياع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some passing caravan means a traveling company; the definite forms for caravan and well are generic, and the vague 'some' helps sell the proposal by promising Joseph will disappear without a trace.
rows.anchor: ( بعض السيارة ( أي بعض جماعة تسير في الأرض وأل في السيارة كما في الجب

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan reads the verb for picking up in the feminine, matching the sense of the caravan as a collective; he cites Arabic poetic usage for a collective noun treated as feminine.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن تلتقطه على التأنيث باعتبار المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional phrase means either 'if you are resolved to separate him from his father' or 'if you will follow my counsel'; the speaker proposes rather than commands, to win the others over.
rows.anchor: أي إن كنتم عازمين مصرين على أن تفعلوا به ما يفرق بينه وبين أبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Jacob 'our father' invokes kinship, and the rhetorical 'what is the matter with you?' expresses surprise; their phrasing shows they had earlier asked to take Joseph and Jacob refused.
rows.anchor: خاطبوه عليه السلام بذلك تحريكا لسلسلة النسب وتذكيرا لرابطة الأخوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They claim sincere goodwill and protection; both clauses are circumstantial, and 'naṣihūn' means they intend good and feel concern for Joseph.
rows.anchor: مريدون له الخير ومشفقون عليه ليس فينا ما يخل بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers assimilate the nūns in taʾmannā with ishām; other readings include assimilation without ishām, a transferred vowel, two pronounced nūns, and the dialect form taymanna.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور ( لا تأمنا ) بالإدغام والإشمال وفسر بضم الشفتين

rows.speaker: أبو رزين
rows.claim: After Abu Ruzayn read the dialect form before ʿUbayd ibn Faḍlah, who called it a mistake, Abu Ruzayn replied that a person reading in his people's dialect has not erred.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر وأبو الشيخ عن عاصم أنه قرأ بذلك بمحضر عبيد بن فضلة فقال له : لحنت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghadan is a temporal adverb for the next day or future time generally; its original final consonant was dropped.
rows.anchor: نصب على الظرفية الزمانية وهو يطلق على اليوم الذي يلي يومك وعلى الزمن المستقبل مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yartaʿ means to eat and drink freely in abundance, originally of animals grazing in plenty; for people it can imply plentiful eating.
rows.anchor: وأصل معنى الرتع أن تأكل وتشرب ما تشاء في خصب وسعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Play here means races, archery, and similar training for fighting, not frivolous amusement; they invoke a form suitable to Joseph's childhood.
rows.anchor: بالاستباق والانتضال ونحوهما مما يتدرب به لقتال العدو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings vary between third-person and first-person forms of yartaʿ/yartʿ and yalʿab, including different endings and whether the final yāʾ is retained; most use jussives.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور ( يرتع ويلعب ) بالياء والجزم والإبنان وأبو عمرو بالنون والجزم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, and Ibn Muhaysin read first-person forms; the author says the readings omit the object, such as livestock, and Ibn Zayd explains the sense through grazing or tending animals.
rows.anchor: والقراءتان على حذف المفعول أي نرتع المواشي أو غيرها والفعلان

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAli reads both verbs in the passive, with ghadan understood as their agent after an omitted preposition; a kasra reading can instead derive from mutual watching, as Mujahid reports.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي رضي الله تعالى عنهما ( يرتع ويلعب ) بالياء والبناء للمفعول

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya calls retaining the final yāʾ in the jussive impermissible except in poetry; al-Alusi answers that dropping a final vowel is a dialect, not poetic necessity.
rows.anchor: وضعف ابن عطية القراءة بإثبات الياء وقال : إن إثباتها في مثل هذا الموضع لا يجوز إلا في الشعر

rows.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
rows.claim: Abu al-Shaykh reports that Muqatil ibn Hayyan read 'we relax and play.'
rows.anchor: وأخرج أبو الشيخ عن مقاتل بن حيان أنه كان يقرأ نلهو ونلعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their promise means they will protect Joseph from harm; the clause is circumstantial. Al-Alusi rejects Abu Hayyan's analysis through the chapter of competing government because circumstantial clauses are not implicit.
rows.anchor: أي من أن يناله مكروه والجملة في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their assurance is reinforced by a nominal sentence, inna, the lām, assigning the duty to all of them, and fronting 'for him.'
rows.anchor: وقد أكدوا مقالتهم بأصناف التأكيد من إيراد الجملة إسمية وتحليتها بأن واللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's reply is an explanatory resumption: Joseph's departure grieves him because separation is hard and he has little patience without him.
rows.anchor: لشدة مفارقته علي وقلة صبري عنه

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: The lām before a present-tense predicate of inna may restrict it to the present, as Sibawayh appears to say; others allow it for present and non-present time, citing 16:124.
rows.anchor: واللام الداخلة على خبر إن إذا كان مضارعا قيل : تقصره على الحال وهو ظاهر كلام سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians object that future departure cannot be the present subject of grief; proposed solutions supply 'your intention/expectation to go' or treat the future departure as conceived now.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأن التقدير قصد أو توقع أن تذهبوا به فالكلام على تقدير المضاف

rows.speaker: شهاب
rows.claim: Shihab calls the grammatical objection a fallacy: people grieve or rejoice about future events, and the linguistic subject need not already exist; al-Alusi responds that a true agent must be something present in or occurring from its subject.
rows.anchor: وقال شهاب : ذلك التحقيق أظن ما قالوه في توجيه الإشكال مغلطة لا أصل لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Hurmuz, Ibn Muhaysin, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read liyaḥzunī with assimilation; Zayd also reads tuḏhibūhu causatively, with the bāʾ of bihi analyzed as extra by Abu Hayyan.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن هرمز وابن محيصن ليحزني بالإدغام وبذلك قرأ زيد بن علي

rows.speaker: الربيع بن ضبع الفزاري
rows.claim: The wolf is an ordinary beast; some say Canaan had many wolves, and its smallness implies Jacob feared still greater predators. A poem by al-Rabiʿ ibn Ḍabʿ says even an aged man fears a wolf.
rows.anchor: ولحقارة الذئب خصه الربيع بن ضبع الفزاري في كونه يخشاه لما بلغ من السن

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say Jacob had dreamed a wolf attacked Joseph; prophetic dreams may occur as seen, while otherwise a wolf in a dream can signify an enemy.
rows.anchor: وقيل : لأنه عليه السلام رأى في المنام أن ذئبا قد شد عليه فكان يحذره

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some allege Jacob used 'wolf' as a veiled reference to one of the brothers; al-Alusi objects that Jacob knew the categories of dreams, while the proposed analogy with Abraham's dream is problematic.
rows.anchor: وادعى بعضهم أنه عليه السلام ورى بالذئب عن واحد منهم فإنه عليه السلام أجل قدرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reported dream of ten wolves surrounding Joseph and the earth swallowing him has no dependable chain, and al-Alusi sees no need to speculate about it.
rows.anchor: وأنا لم أجد لرواية الرؤيا مطلقا سندا يعول عليه ولا حاجة بنا إلى اعتبارها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's words may have been an unintentional prompt for the brothers' eventual lie, like the cited rebuke in 82:6; as the proverb says, misfortune is tied to speech.
rows.anchor: ما وقع منه عليه السلام من هذا القول كأن تلقينا للجواب من غير قصد

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports the Prophet warning not to prompt people to lie: Jacob's sons did not know wolves ate people until their father supplied that excuse.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أبو الشيخ وغيره عن ابن عمر رضي الله تعالى عنهما قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم : لا تلقنوا الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grief is pain at losing what one loves, while fear is agitation at expected harm; grief attaches to Joseph's departure, fear to the possibility of a wolf attack.
rows.anchor: والحزن ألم القلب لفوت المحبوب والخوف انزعاج النفس لنزول المكروه

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi, Khalaf, Abu Jaʿfar, Warsh, and others replace the hamza in dhiʾb with yāʾ by the regular sound change; reciters differ between pausal and connected forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكسائي وخلف وأبو جعفر وورش والأعشى وغيرهم بإبدالها ياءا لسكونها وانكسار ما قبلها

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari derives the wolf's name from wind blowing from every direction; al-Asmaʿi derives the wind expression from the wolf's charging, which al-Alusi finds more apt despite an objection about deriving verbs from fixed nouns.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصمعي : إن اشتقاق تذاءبت من الذئب لأن الذئب يفعله في عدوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'While you are heedless' means while distracted by grazing and play or insufficiently attentive to guarding Joseph.
rows.anchor: لإشتغالكم بالرتع واللعب أو لقلة اهتمامكم بحفظه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their oath condition says they are a group able to handle crises; the lām introduces an oath, and the following statement is its answer.
rows.anchor: أي والحال أنا جماعة جديرة بأن تعصب بنا الأمور وتكفي بآرائنا وتدبيراتنا الخطوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāsirūn may mean ruined, weak and incapable, deserving destruction or a curse, or literally having lost their livestock by failing to protect them.
rows.anchor: والخسار إما بمهنى الهلاك أو تجويزا عن الضعف أو استحقاقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They answer only the wolf concern because it is the stronger reason for refusal; sadness is brief, follows from fear, or is something they deliberately ignore because it concerns Joseph's favored status.
rows.anchor: لأنه السبب القوي في المنع دون الحزن لقصر زمانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers firmly resolved to put Joseph in the well; reported locations include near Canaan, between Egypt and Midian, and Jordan, while Jerusalem is rejected because the distance conflicts with same-day caravan pickup.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أنها بئر بيت المقدس وتعقب بأنه يرده التعليل بالتقاط بعض السيارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer to lammā is omitted for obviousness and because the event resists concise telling; it may be summarized as their doing what they did or as their great trial. An analysis making 'We revealed' the answer with an extra wāw is rejected.
rows.anchor: وجواب لما محذوف إيذانا بظهوره وإشعارا بأن تفصيله مما لا يحويه فلك العبارة

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: A long account from Wahb and other historians says the brothers obtained permission by proposing a livestock outing, then beat and threatened Joseph; Judah stopped Reuben from killing him and proposed the well instead.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب وغيره من أهل السير والأخبار : إن إخوة يوسف عليه السلام قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another version says they lowered Joseph in a bucket and dropped him midway intending to kill him; he fell into the water and stood on a rock.
rows.anchor: وقيل : جعلوه في دلو ثم أدلوه فلما بلغ نصفها ألقوه إرادة أن يموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the narrative, Joseph clung to the well's rim, was bound and stripped of his shirt, pleaded for it, and was thrown in; his brothers mocked his plea for company.
rows.anchor: فقال : يا إخوتاه ردوا علي قميصي لأستتر به في الجب فلم يفعلوا ثم ألقوه فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports say Judah prevented the brothers from crushing Joseph with a stone; an angel clothed him in Abraham's heavenly shirt, illuminating the well. Hasan says its water became sweet and Gabriel comforted him.
rows.anchor: وكان عند يعقوب قميص إبراهيم عليه السلام الذي كساه الله تعالى إياه من الجنة

rows.speaker: محمد بن مسلم الطائفي
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Muslim al-Taʾifi says Joseph prayed for relief from his distress; other versions give prayers asking for mercy and rescue.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن مسلم الطائفي : إنه عليه السلام لما ألقي في الجب قال

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Mardawayh transmits from Ibn ʿUmar a prophetic report in which Gabriel teaches Joseph a prayer in the well; God grants escape and later rule in Egypt, and the Prophet urges frequent recitation.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن مردويه عن ابن عمر قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم : لما ألقي يوسف في الجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the many accounts about the well and its prayers are moving, but none has a chain on which he can rely.
rows.anchor: والروايات في كيفية إلقائه وما قال : وما قيل له كثيرة وقد تضمنت ما يلين له الصخر لكن ليس فيها ما له سند يعود عليه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says God inspired Joseph in the well; another view says he received glad dreams, while al-Dahhak and Qatada say Gabriel was sent to him.
rows.anchor: وكان ذلك على ما روي عن مجاهد بالإلهام وقيل : بالإلقاء في مبشرات المنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation consoles Joseph and promises he will escape and later tell his brothers what they did, without their recognizing him.
rows.anchor: أي أعلمناه عند ذلك تبشيرا له بما يؤول إليه أمره وإزالة لوحشته وتسلية له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'While they do not perceive' most naturally means they will fail to recognize Joseph because his future authority and their changed circumstances make recognition implausible; this better consoles him than the alternative.
rows.anchor: والأول أدخل في التسلية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that when Joseph's brothers later entered Egypt, he recognized them but they did not; he tapped the cup, which revealed their past crime, and Ibn ʿAbbas connects this with the prophecy.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير وابن أبي حاتم عن ابن عباس قال : لما دخل إخوة يوسف على يوسف

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada allows 'they do not perceive' to describe their ignorance that revelation was comforting Joseph and relieving his loneliness.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يتعلق ( وهم لا يشعرون ) بالإيحاء على معنى أنا آنسناه بالوحي

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Authorities differ on Joseph's age at the revelation: al-Dahhak says six, al-Hasan twelve or eighteen, and Ibn al-Saʾib seventeen; al-Alusi infers he was likely not yet pubescent, and in any case under forty.
rows.anchor: وكان هذا الإيحاء وهو عليه السرم ابن ست عند الضحاك واثنتي عشرة سنة أو ثماني عشرة سنة عند الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that the pronoun in 'We revealed to him' refers to Jacob is untenable.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن ضمير ( إليه ) يعود على يعقوب عليه السلام وليس بشيء

rows.speaker: ابن عمرو
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmr reads the future verb in the third person, as in Basran codices; Salam reads it as a threat, which affects how 'they do not perceive' attaches, and a proposed alternative linkage is challenged.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عمرو رضي الله تعالى عنهما لينبئنهم بياء الغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A traveling caravan came to the well from Midian toward Egypt after three days, or according to another view the second day; the well was likely on their usual route, though some place it in a remote wilderness.
rows.anchor: وكان ذلك بعد ثلاثة أيام مضت من زمن إلقائه في قوله وقيل : في اليوم الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They sent their water-drawer, Malik ibn Dhaʿr al-Khuzaʿi; Ibn ʿAtiyya allows the word for water-drawer to mean one person or a group, but al-Alusi prefers the singular.
rows.anchor: وكان ذلك مالك بن ذعر الخزاعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine 'came' agrees with caravan by sense, while 'they sent' and 'their water-drawer' agree by form; the omitted objects of 'came' and 'sent' are understood from context.
rows.anchor: ( جاءت ) والتذكير في ( أرسلوا و واردهم ) باعتبار اللفظ والمعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb 'came' hints at Joseph's honor with God; the water-drawer lowered his bucket into the well, and the text omits that Joseph clung to it and came out.
rows.anchor: وفي التعبير بالمجيء إيماء إلى كرامة يوسف عليه السلام عند ربه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bucket is usually grammatically feminine, though some usages vary; the source details its diminutive and plurals and distinguishes it from the masculine verbal noun dalw.
rows.anchor: والدلو من المؤنثات للسماعية فتصغر على دلية وتجمع على أدل ودلاء ودلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cry 'O my good news, here is a boy!' personifies glad tidings as someone summoned, or may be an ordinary exclamation; the suggestion that Bushra is a companion's name is rejected.
rows.anchor: نادى البشرى بشارة لنفسه أو لقومه ورفقته كأنه نزلها منزلة شخص فناداه

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi is cited for the view that Bushra was the name of the water-drawer's companion, but al-Alusi rejects it.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن بشرى اسم صاحب له ناداه ليعينه على إخراجه وروي هذا السدي

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Non-Kufan readers add the possessive yāʾ in yā bushrāy; Hamza and al-Kisaʾi use imālah, Warsh a sound between, and other readers vary the yāʾ or merge it, with Abu Dhuʾayb's poetry illustrating the dialect.
rows.anchor: وقرأ غير الكوفيين يا بشراي بالإضافة وأمال فتحة الراء حمزة والكسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghulām usually means a boy from age two until puberty, but can also refer to a fully grown man, as in Layla al-Akhyaliyya's description of al-Hajjaj.
rows.anchor: الغلام كثيرا ما يطلق على ما بين الحولين إلى البلوغ وقد يطلق على الرجل الكامل
